title: Protocols and protocol-oriented programming
summary: A protocol is a contract: "anything that conforms can do these things". Swift prefers small protocols plus extensions over deep class inheritance.
body: **In simple words:** A protocol lists requirements (methods, properties). Any struct, class or enum can promise to meet them. Code that works with the protocol does not care which concrete type it gets.
**Real-life analogy:** A power socket. Any device with the right plug (conformance) works, whether it is a lamp or a laptop.

**Protocol extensions** give default implementations, so many types share behavior without a common base class. That is the core of protocol-oriented programming (POP): compose behavior from small protocols (`Identifiable & Codable & Hashable`) instead of building a deep inheritance tree.

**Why POP over inheritance:** works with structs and enums (inheritance only works with classes), a type can conform to many protocols but inherit from only one class, and you avoid the "fragile base class" problem.
**Associated types** make a protocol generic: `Collection` has an `Element`. Such protocols are used with generics (`some Collection<Int>`) or `any`.
**Testing:** depend on a protocol (`protocol FeedAPI`) instead of a concrete class; tests pass a fake that conforms.

**Common standard protocols:** `Equatable` (==), `Hashable` (usable in Set/Dictionary keys), `Comparable` (<, sorting), `Identifiable` (stable `id`, used by SwiftUI lists), `Codable` (JSON), `Sendable` (safe across threads), `CustomStringConvertible`.
keyPoints: Protocols define capabilities; extensions add default behavior; types compose many small protocols.
POP works for value types and avoids single-inheritance limits.
Depending on protocols makes code testable through dependency injection.
Gotcha: methods defined only in an extension (not in the protocol body) are statically dispatched and cannot be overridden through the protocol.
Mark delegate protocols `AnyObject` so the delegate can be held `weak`.

code.caption: Default implementation and composition

mistakes: Huge "god protocols" with many requirements; split them.
Expecting an extension-only method to be overridden when called through the protocol type.
Creating a protocol for every single class "just in case" - add one when you need a second implementation or a test seam.
followups: **Protocol vs abstract class?** Swift has no abstract classes; protocols + extensions cover the same need and work for structs.
**What is `Self` in a protocol?** The conforming type. Protocols using `Self` (like `Equatable`) need generics or `any` with care.
**Why `AnyObject` on delegate protocols?** Only classes can be `weak`.
